canberra.title: Clayface is as terrifying and brutal as comic book movies get
canberra.snippet: Comic book movies based on supervillains very rarely work. With the exception of Joaquin Phoenix’s first Joker film, most are shall...
canberra.content:
Clayface is based on the DC supervillain of the same name and is the newest movie in the superhero franchise. Photo: Warner Bros.

Comic book movies based on supervillains very rarely work.

With the exception of Joaquin Phoenix’s first Joker film, most are shallow, mediocre outings released to make a quick buck.

Since 2017, we’ve had three Venom films, none of which were great. Kraven, which is somehow worse and Morbius, which, if you haven’t seen it, consider yourself blessed.

With the track record of supervillain movies being rocky, to say the least, you’d have to be very ambitious or greedy to pull from that well again, right?

But despite being only two movies deep into their brand-new comic book universe, DC Studios thought it was worth the risk, so we have a new horror movie based on the obscure Batman villain Clayface.

Clayface follows Matt Hagan (Tom Rhys Harries), a Gotham City actor who celebrates recently winning an Academy Award by hitting the club. Matt meets Mia Torrez (Joana Ribeiro), the girlfriend of feared mob boss Markos Szabo (David Dencik).

Even after being warned about her criminal links, Matt spends the night with Mia. An enraged Markos then gets payback by disfiguring Matt’s face with a knife.

Left scarred, Matt is desperate to return to his life of fame and fortune. He turns to a new and untested experimental procedure that allows him to repair his face.

While it initially seems successful, things quickly get worse, and Matt’s skin slowly turns into a clay-like substance. Now angry and mangled but with new abilities, Matt decides to instead hunt down those who wronged him.

As a film, in a word, Clayface is brutal.

Unlike almost every superhero movie I’ve ever seen, Clayface uses its MA rating to deliver a truly violent, gory and unpleasant experience. A particular moment set in a bathroom on an aeroplane will sit with me for weeks.

These moments make the film stand out and separate it from other films in the genre. It doesn’t try to redeem its main character like other villain-focused films do, and it’s not interested in being kid-friendly.

Unfortunately, the movie’s narrative doesn’t match the quality of its gross-out moments. Harries is great as Matt, and he does well with the script he’s given, but there’s only so much he can do with a very standard revenge story.

This makes the movie more of an experience than a film. Audiences will see Clayface, cover their eyes, scream out loud and do their best not to squirm in a cinema, but they won’t revisit it once they’ve seen it.

At the movie’s best, it’s a comic-book version of 2024’s The Substance and David Cronenberg’s The Fly. At its worst, it’s a run-of-the-mill revenge plot, like a straight-to-streaming action flick.

For the most part, the visual gags are horrifically fantastic. It really does create the feeling that this man is slowly turning to mush. They make the movie truly worth watching, if you can stomach it.

The score is also pretty solid, and the production really makes the underbelly of the famous Gotham City pop.

It’s worth touching on where Batman fits into all of this. DC Studios has confirmed he is in the universe and Gotham is his home. However, there is no mention of him throughout the movie.

Fans who want the Caped Crusader to come up against Matt should temper their expectations, because it doesn’t happen here.

All these factors make for a slightly above-average horror outing.

The gore and the horror elements are very strong and Harries is a very entertaining lead. The faults are solely script-based.

If you want horror, Clayface is worth the price of admission. If you’re after something a little deeper, maybe wait until it hits HBO Max in the new year.

Clayface is showing in cinemas now.

canberra.title: 57 deaths, 20-day median: What Canberra’s first assisted dying report reveals
canberra.snippet: For someone nearing the end of their life even a short journey to a doctor’s appointment can be an ordeal. Yet in Canberra, people ...
canberra.content:
The ACT government has marked one year of voluntary assisted dying, with new figures showing 57 people accessed the scheme in its first eight months. Photo: Palliative Care Australia.

For someone nearing the end of their life even a short journey to a doctor’s appointment can be an ordeal. Yet in Canberra, people seeking voluntary assisted dying may still have to travel for consultations that could otherwise take place over the phone or by video.

It is one of the biggest barriers remaining one year after the ACT introduced voluntary assisted dying, with new figures revealing that 57 Canberrans died through the scheme in its first eight months.

The ACT Voluntary Assisted Dying Oversight Board’s inaugural report, released this week (3 November), shows 163 people made an initial request between 3 November 2025 and 30 June 2026.

Of those, 156 underwent a first assessment, 128 had a consulting assessment, 116 made a second request and 110 reached the final request stage.

Approved substances were dispensed in 65 cases, with 57 deaths recorded following administration. The median age of people making an initial request was 77, while the median time between a first request and death was just 20 days.

However, the numbers do not necessarily represent people who abandoned or were refused access to the scheme. Some were still progressing through the process when the reporting period ended.

The oversight board, which reviews cases after they are completed, found no systemic safety concerns during the reporting period.

But while the ACT Government celebrated the first anniversary of the scheme, officials acknowledged that access remains difficult for some of the people it is intended to help.

Attorney-General Tara Cheyne said Commonwealth criminal laws restricting certain voluntary assisted dying conversations over telecommunications were creating unnecessary hardship.

The restrictions stem from federal laws introduced more than two decades ago to address suicide-related material communicated electronically. Ms Cheyne argued those provisions should not prevent medical practitioners from discussing lawful voluntary assisted dying with patients.

For someone who was seriously ill, she said, the inability to have certain conversations remotely could cause considerable distress. Even in a relatively small jurisdiction such as Canberra, travelling to appointments can be difficult for people approaching the end of their lives.

Oversight board chair Darlene Cox agreed that the restrictions were a significant obstacle.

“There’s a lot of public discussion around rural and remote areas, but when you’re at end of life, when you are very unwell, it’s actually very challenging to get to appointments,” she said.

Ms Cheyne said state and territory ministers had been pressing the Commonwealth to address the issue, with further discussions expected at the next meeting of attorneys-general.

The figures also raise questions about the availability of medical professionals willing and trained to participate. According to the report, 43 practitioners completed mandatory training during the first eight months.

Asked whether the existing workforce was sufficient to meet demand, Health Minister Marisa Paterson said the government was continuing to encourage more practitioners to become involved.

“We are always looking for more clinicians who would like to be involved in supporting the community through voluntary assisted dying,” she said.

Unlike some other Australian jurisdictions, the ACT does not require a person to be within a specified timeframe of death to qualify, although strict eligibility criteria apply.

There are also no mandatory waiting periods between the stages of the process and nurse practitioners can undertake assessments as authorised practitioners.

Dr Paterson said the government was proud of the scheme’s first year but acknowledged further work was needed. One unresolved issue involves people who have been approved for voluntary assisted dying but subsequently lose the capacity to make decisions.

Under the current framework, maintaining decision-making capacity is an important requirement for accessing the scheme.

The ACT Government is preparing a citizens’ jury to consider how the law should respond when an eligible person has clearly expressed a wish to access assisted dying but loses capacity before completing the process.

The jury’s recommendations could shape future changes to the legislation, with a broader review scheduled for 2028.

Meanwhile, Palliative Care ACT has called for better integration between palliative care and voluntary assisted dying, rather than treating them as competing options.

Chief executive officer Paul Arztenhofer said the anniversary provided an opportunity to examine how patients, families and health professionals could be better supported. He also called for stronger support for the palliative care workforce.

canberra.title: The more I learn, the less I know: Expanding my viewpoint exposed chasms of ignorance
canberra.snippet: I attended the Blue Mountains Writers Festival in Katoomba last weekend and estimate I am 78 per cent smarter for the experience. I’m def...
canberra.content:
Benjamin Law and Michael Mohammed Admad helped make Haylet at least 78 per cent smarter. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

I attended the Blue Mountains Writers Festival in Katoomba last weekend and estimate I am 78 per cent smarter for the experience.

I’m definitely feeling brighter, in any case.

Not a natural scholar, my university experience felt more like learning by osmosis. I flitted in and out of classes between bar crawls, music festivals and the multiple jobs I had to work to support such a lifestyle.

Now, all grown up, it was a treat to dive into an intensive learning environment. But in doing so, I uncovered cavernous holes in my knowledge. I approached with intrigue.

My first session immediately set the scene for a steep learning curve. It was the ABC’s Benjamin Law in conversation with Miles Franklin-shortlisted author Michael Mohammed Ahmad.

Mohammed is an award-winning novelist with a PhD in creative writing, as well as the founding director of Sweatshop Literacy Movement, a not-for-profit organisation supporting writers from Indigenous and non-English-speaking backgrounds.

So – shock me – he was a fountain of knowledge. For me, he was also a window to other worlds. My experience as an audience member was effectively one long ‘Aha!’ moment. I’m still absorbing half of what was shared.

One particularly mind-expanding realisation was about the relationship between language and our perception of reality.

Known as ‘linguistic relativity’, it refers to how language can influence how its speakers think, perceive and move through the world.

To illustrate his point, Mohammed showed how Arabic identifies cousin relationships with great specificity, detailing parental, sibling and gender lineage. He contrasted that with other cultures that use much broader language around family.

He drew a fascinating line between these linguistics and different cultural approaches to the ‘acceptability’ of marriage within family lines.

As an English speaker, this blew my monolingual mind.

I looked around the room with interest, wondering what parallel universes of understanding were among us.

Whipping out my phone, I did some quick research and found several examples.

Russian features distinct words for light and dark blue, and research suggests its speakers distinguish such shades faster than English speakers.

Here in Australia, the Indigenous Guugu Yimithirr language uses north/south/east/west rather than ‘left/right’, with many positing that this helps speakers maintain a continuous sense of orientation.

When accidents occur, English tends to emphasise who caused the problem – John broke the vase – whereas Japanese speakers are more inclined to focus on the event – the vase broke – often leaving the human out entirely.

As a vase-breaker from way back, I appreciate this grammatical trickery.

A first-hand example comes to mind in the way Spanish treats age.

While I consider myself an English-only speaker, I did gain a half-decent grasp of Spanish for a time, when travelling in South America.

In English, I am 40 years old. It has permanence. It is a state of my being.

In Spanish, the phrase is ‘Tengo 40 años’, which literally translates as ‘I have 40 years’. Age is something I have accumulated, not what I am.

Another tick from me!

A word of warning on this Spanish phrase. It should not be confused with ‘Tengo 40 anos’, which carries a completely different, anatomical meaning. A lesson I unfortunately learnt in casual conversation with a small Peruvian child, whose version of reality was forever altered.

Sometimes it’s the absence of words which influences us.

Back at the festival, Pip Williams, author of The Dictionary of Lost Words, The Bookbinder of Jericho and now The German Ward, touched on how things that go unrecorded can impact our understanding of history.

In fact, her debut novel was inspired by the word “bondmaid” (a female slave forced to serve without wages) and its exclusion from the first edition of the Oxford English Dictionary.

My mind spun as I grappled with our vulnerable history books and the unperceived truths beyond my reach. As the saying goes, “You don’t know what you don’t know”.

Overall, my enlightening weekend was a good reminder that – among the rhythms and routines of our daily grind – it’s easy to fall into an echo chamber.

Or less “fall”, more “sink gradually, without realising”.

Daily life keeps us busy, often moving through familiar spaces and having familiar conversations with familiar faces.

For my part, I’m going to make more of an effort to crawl out of my comfortable chamber and seek new horizons.

Because I left the festival feeling decidedly smarter – or at least, more aware of how little I know.

canberra.title: 6 reasons to love Sapling Yard’s new cellar door (hint: they’re all wine)
canberra.snippet: It’s been a big year for local boutique winery Sapling Yard. Founder and winemaker Carla Rodeghiero (along with her co-winemaker Malcolm ...
canberra.content:
The Sapling Yard Cellar Door is a lovely spot to enjoy a tasting in the sun with snacks from neighbouring Aranya Acres. Photo: Martin Conway.

It’s been a big year for local boutique winery Sapling Yard.

Founder and winemaker Carla Rodeghiero (along with her co-winemaker Malcolm Burdett) picked up a trophy at the National Wine Show earlier this year and have now shifted their cellar door to be co-located with their winemaking facilities out at Aranya Acres.

I had visited the Aranya Acres restaurant (formerly the site of Contentious Character) at Wamboin shortly after they opened. The Sapling Yard Cellar door feels appropriately ‘cellar-ish’, tucked under the main restaurant building.

Visiting on a sunny Saturday, the dappled shade in the courtyard formed the perfect backdrop for a tasting. We were given the option of low tables or high-top bars and decided to perch on stools at a wine barrel.

The standard tasting is 6 glasses. You can choose your own drops, or have the staff pick for you. We let the lovely Rachelle guide us, and we’re glad we did.

Get yourself a grazing board and settle in for a great afternoon. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

But first: snacks.

The antipasto board on offer here is a serious affair: gorgeous squid-ink salami, oozy soft cheese, fiery ‘nduja salami, olives, pickled fennel, and some juicy figs. Absolutely spot on, and totally delicious.

The cellar door menu comes from the Aranya Acres kitchen, and you can also enjoy oysters, sardines and something called ‘ultimate garlic bread’ that sounds utterly vampire-proof.

To start, Rachelle poured us a taste of the Entrachet, a sparkling wine made in the classic Champagne style. Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Meunier grapes are used for this wine, which is left ‘on lees’ (in contact with yeast residue) for 18 months. This lets the wine develop those toasty brioche flavours you’d expect in a Champagne. It’s dry, refreshing and oh-so-drinkable on a hot day!

At this point in our tasting, we were visited by the local wildlife: a fellow diner initially warned us of a snake moving our way, but it turned out to be a friendly (and fat!) blue tongue lizard.

Sapling Yard winemakers Malcolm Burdett and Carla Rodeghiero won a trophy at the National Wine Show for their Fiori wine. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Our only request for the tasting was for a Riesling – to quote my plus-one, “I’d kill for a cheeky Riesling right about now!”. To avoid any wine-related homicides, Rachelle happily complied.

Made with grapes from Lake George, this wine is everything you want from a Canberra region Riesling. Dry, acidic, refreshing and full of punchy lime and green apple notes, with just a touch of blossom.

Speaking of blossom: up next we tasted the Fiori, the white blend that won Sapling Yard their trophy.

I’ve had this wine before, and every time I am delighted by the perfume of this delicate drop. Gewürztraminer grapes add a musky, sticky sweetness, while Pinot Gris adds crisp pear, and Pinot Blanc and Riesling balance everything out with a little citric acidity. It’s unique, really delicious and an absolute bargain at $32 a bottle.

We rounded out the tasting with a few reds.

The Shiraz Viognier – a wine I always associate with Canberra region makers – is a top-notch example of the style. The Gamay and Montepulciano were both bold and flavourful, but still light enough to enjoy on a hot day.

Each of the six wines we tasted was either a perfect example of its style, or a whole new expression of what Canberra Region wines can be. For my money, Carla is making some of the region’s best wines.

We rounded out our visit with a wander through some creative bird statues on the lawns. You can also book a full tour of the winery if you’d like a behind-the-scenes peek at how things are done.

Sapling Yard Cellar Door is located at 810 Norton Road, Wamboin, adjacent to Aranya Acres restaurant. They are open for tastings on Saturday from 11 am to 5 pm and Sunday from 12 pm to 4 pm. Reservations are recommended (especially if you’d like a tour). Follow Sapling Yard on Facebook or Instagram.

canberra.title: Petrol or plug-in hybrid? We compare two similar but very different Mitsubishi Outlanders
canberra.snippet: Same age. Same income. Same starting balance. The difference? One Mitsubishi Outlander in this seemingly identical pair packs a perfectly...
canberra.content:
8 November 2026

Join the conversation

5

Although they look almost identical, the PHEV (left) and petrol (right) versions of the Mitsubishi Outlander deliver vastly different experiences. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia (edited with AI).

Same age. Same income. Same starting balance. The difference? One Mitsubishi Outlander in this seemingly identical pair packs a perfectly conventional petrol engine, while the other is a thrifty plug-in hybrid.

But just how do these two fuel types compare? In the ACT, and indeed across Australia, plug-in hybrids are the least popular type of new vehicle sold.

However, PHEV sales have increased in recent months, while sales of internal combustion engine vehicles are going downhill.

Some will argue that opting for a PHEV is a bit like being a fence-sitter; it screams, “I wanted an EV but have too much range anxiety”.

It’s a solution I’ve long been a fan of, though – so long as you understand how to get the best out of a PHEV, which does require more thought.

To compare the pair and see whether it really makes sense for more buyers to switch from pure petrol to a PHEV, I spent time in two almost identical Mitsubishi Outlanders.

Why the Outlander? In 2014, the previous-generation model was the first plug-in hybrid SUV to be sold in Australia. It was also the first PHEV I ever drove, and the first to offer a glimpse of its genuine future viability.

That future, clearly, is now.

The petrol Outlander got a facelift in 2025, which carried over to the PHEV model in 2026. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What is it?

The Mitsubishi Outlander doesn’t need much of an introduction. It’s consistently been one of the best-selling SUVs in the country, and among the top-sellers in any category.

It recently received a number of commendable changes to freshen it up, including a new suspension and steering setup honed on the roads of South Australia to better suit Aussie conditions.

For this comparison, we’ve got the one you really want: the top-spec Outlander Exceed Tourer, finished in Moonstone Grey with lavish brick brown semi-aniline leather.

Whatever on earth semi-aniline means, I can tell you it’s very lovely.

The Exceed Tourer scores the best upgrades. A set of baller 20-inch diamond-cut alloys complement the Outlander’s refreshed looks, with revised bumpers and smoked rear tail-lights.

Inside, you’ll now find a bangin’ 12-speaker premium Yamaha audio system that’s among the best out there, which has been added to a cabin that already featured luxuries as extensive as massage seats. Yep, in a humble Mitsi!

Mind you, this Mitsubishi isn’t so humble when it comes to the price tag.

The conventional petrol model packs a 2.5-litre four-pot that serves up 135kW. With standard all-wheel drive in this spec, it asks for $57,990 before on-road costs.

In the top-spec Outlander Exceed Tourer on test here, you’ll find a gorgeous brick brown leather interior. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

By contrast, the PHEV offers over 63 per cent more power from its 221kW hybrid system, utilising a 2.4-litre engine and two electric motors. However, it commands a $74,490 price tag – a 28 per cent price jump.

The savings are promised through a drastic reduction in fuel consumption. The petrol’s 8.1L/100km claim falls to just 1.2L/100km for the PHEV. My testing revealed 8.6L/100km and 1.9L/100km in the real world, respectively.

At the average Canberra fuel price of 206.5 cents a litre, the dearest in the country during Q3 2026 according to FuelRadar, it will take over 115,000 km of driving to break even on the price difference between them – and that’s before factoring the additional cost of charging.

The upside is that the Outlander PHEV has an impressive 103 km of electric-only driving range – a claim which isn’t too far-fetched.

Despite their vastly different underpinnings, there aren’t many ways to tell the two apart, aside from the extra badging on the PHEV’s boot and front doors.

The only other change is there being a filler flap on both sides of the PHEV model. Weirdly, the petrol filler even moves from the right side to the left, while the flap on the right side is bigger. Producing four totally different rear quarter panels can’t be too cheap.

Additional badging on the doors and boot lid are one of the only ways to tell the PHEV apart. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Badging across the bonnet... just like a Range Rover. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

20-inch alloys are standard on this top-spec model. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

The Outlander PHEV accepts both Type 2 and CHAdeMO chargers. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Additional badging on the doors and boot lid are one of the only ways to tell the PHEV apart. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

From a low-enough angle, you might spot the battery pack underneath the Outlander PHEV. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Blink and you'll miss the differences on this petrol model when compared to the PHEV. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia.

The Outlander now features a local suspension and steering tune, developed on the roads of South Australia. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia.

The Outlander PHEV uses a 2.4-litre engine with two electric motors, delivering a healthy 221kW. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What’s it like to live with?

If there’s one thing that’s $16,500 better about the Outlander PHEV, it’s the way it drives.

The regular-degular petrol model has been vastly improved thanks to the new, localised suspension setup. It’s a pretty sweet thing to steer.

But the PHEV, thanks to its additional weight and lower centre of gravity, is even better. It simply feels more settled on the road, and even a bit more premium than the already impressive ‘normal’ model. There’s a reason our subconscious associates heavier things with being more luxurious.

The PHEV is also far punchier thanks to its instant electric power, and far smoother thanks to how those electric motors deliver it.

To really extract the most out of the PHEV, though, you’ll need to put your thinking cap on, rather than simply getting in and sliding the leather-clad shifter into D.

Between the shifter and drive mode dial, the PHEV has two extra buttons. The one on the left turns on one-pedal driving, which ramps up regenerative braking, so it should come to a stop without using the brake pedal.

The other button, marked ‘EV’, is the one you’ll really need to pay attention to. For most people, leaving it in Normal mode will be fine, especially in a place like Canberra. If you have a longer commute or plan on taking a road trip, however, you might want to play around with it.

The front seats offer heating, ventilation, and even massage functions. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

The rear seats are also heated. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

There are three different seat massage programs to choose from, with different intensity levels. Photo: Mitsubishi Motors Australia.

The Yamaha premium audio system is among the best out there. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

In addition to seven drive modes, there is also one-pedal driving and four powertrain configurations to choose from. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Instead of a tachometer, the PHEV model gets a gauge that shows regenerative braking, EV power, and petrol power usage. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

There are four powertrain settings: Normal, EV, Save, and Charge. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Put it into Save when you’re on a freeway or long country road, and it will run the petrol engine (which operates more efficiently than an electric motor at high speeds) and preserve your battery charge for city streets.

When you get there, pop it into EV mode, and it will use the electric motors in their most efficient environment, instead of keeping a petrol engine idling pointlessly.

If you forget to do either and leave it in Normal, it will churn through a battery charge on the freeway; there’s even a Charge mode that uses the petrol engine like a generator to top the battery back up.

A little bit of thought goes a long way.

The verdict

There’s little question in my mind, at least, that the PHEV is the better Outlander of the two tested here. Smoother, more powerful, far more efficient. No qualms there.

Whether it’s worth the extra cost comes down not only to how you plan to use it, but how long you plan to keep it.

If you know you’ll keep this thing for a while – worth doing with Mitsubishi offering up to 10 years of warranty coverage if you service at an authorised dealership – then you’ll make back those savings by the time you come to upgrade.

It’s also worth keeping in mind that while novated leasing deals for PHEVs like the Outlander have been exempt from fringe benefits tax, there are increasing calls for this subsidy scheme to be scrapped at the time of writing.

However, if you’re the sort of person who upgrades your car regularly, you simply won’t see a return on those savings unless you’re on the open road all day, where the PHEV makes less sense anyway.

In a place like Canberra, though, going PHEV – regardless of what vehicle you’re looking at – makes an awful lot of sense. Thrifty around the roundabouts, yet (almost) thought-free on a drive up to Sydney.

While the petrol Outlander is significantly cheaper than the equivalent PHEV model, each version is clearly suited to a different type of buyer. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

2026 Mitsubishi Outlander Exceed Tourer Petrol

  • $57,990 before on-road costs
  • 2.5-litre four-cylinder, 135 kW/244 Nm
  • CVT, all-wheel drive
  • 8.1 litres per 100km, 55-litre fuel capacity
  • 1695 kg kerb weight.

2026 Mitsubishi Outlander Exceed Tourer PHEV

  • $74,990 before on-road costs
  • 2.4-litre four-cylinder with two electric motors, 221 kW
  • CVT, all-wheel drive
  • 1.2 litres per 100km, 53-litre fuel capacity
  • 103 km electric range, 22.7 kWh battery pack
  • 2158 kg kerb weight.

Thanks to Mitsubishi Motors Australia for providing this vehicle for testing. Region has no commercial arrangement with Mitsubishi Motors Australia.
